e.etymology: A spelling of the surname Hayley or Haley, from an English place name, Old English hieg, hay, plus leah, clearing.
namesakes: Hailey Bieber (model and beauty entrepreneur, wife of Justin Bieber)

e.etymology: The Latin and Greek form of Hebrew Hannah, grace or favor. Its spread across Europe owes most to Saint Anne, by tradition the mother of the Virgin Mary.

assoc.t: Princess Anna, Elsa's sister in Disney's Frozen

e.etymology: The English form of French Madeleine, from Greek Magdalene, the woman from Magdala, a village on the Sea of Galilee whose name means tower. It honors Mary Magdalene.

assoc.t: Madeline, the Paris schoolgirl of the picture books

e.meaning: Greek goddess of wisdom and war
e.etymology: From Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom, war and crafts and the patron of Athens. The name is older than the Greek language and its meaning is unknown.

assoc.t: Greek goddess of wisdom and war

e.etymology: A modern respelling of Jackson, the English surname meaning son of Jack. Jack began as a medieval pet form of John.
From an English surname with two opposite Old English sources: blæc, black or dark, and blac, pale or shining. It can also be an English form of the Irish surname Ó Bláthmaic.
namesakes: Blake Shelton (country singer and longtime coach on The Voice)

e.etymology: From the city of Savannah, Georgia, and its river, or from savanna, a grassy plain, a word English took from Spanish sabana, of Taino origin. The river's own name may come from the Shawnee people.

assoc.t: Savannah, Georgia, historic Southern port city
savanna, a tropical grassland

e.etymology: The English spelling of Welsh Ifan, a form of John, which goes back through Latin and Greek to Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
namesakes: Evan Hansen (title character of the musical Dear Evan Hansen)

e.etymology: From Greek Georgios, from georgos, farmer: ge, earth, plus ergon, work. The dragon-slaying Saint George is the patron of England, and six British kings have borne the name.

assoc.t: Curious George, the storybook monkey

e.etymology: From Norman French Auberi, a form of the Germanic name Alberich, from alb, elf, and rich, ruler. A man's name in medieval England, it has been given mostly to girls in the US since the 1970s.
A spelling of Leila or Lila, from Arabic layla, night. The name reached English through the Arabic and Persian love story of Layla and Majnun and through Byron's poems.
From Hebrew sarah, lady or princess. In Genesis, God renames Abraham's wife Sarai as Sarah when she is promised a son, Isaac.
namesakes: Sarah Jessica Parker (actress, Sex and the City)
Sarah Michelle Gellar (actress, Buffy the Vampire Slayer)
Sarah Palin (former Alaska governor and vice presidential nominee)

assoc.t: Sarah, wife of Abraham in the Bible

e.etymology: From Greek Lydia, a woman from Lydia, an ancient kingdom in what is now western Turkey. In the New Testament, Lydia of Thyatira, a seller of purple cloth, is Paul's first convert in Europe.
namesakes: Lydia Deetz (the goth teenager in Beetlejuice)
Lydia Bennet (the youngest sister in Pride and Prejudice)

e.etymology: Brought into English use by James Fenimore Cooper's The Last of the Mohicans (1826), and usually traced to Greek kore, maiden, a title of the goddess Persephone.
namesakes: Cora Munro (heroine of The Last of the Mohicans)
Cora Crawley (the Countess of Grantham in Downton Abbey)

e.etymology: The Italian feminine form of Gabriel, Hebrew Gavriel, usually read as God is my strength or man of God. Gabriel is the archangel who announces the births of John the Baptist and Jesus.
namesakes: Gabriella Montez (the female lead of High School Musical)

e.meaning: the biblical hill of Jerusalem; a promised land
e.etymology: From Hebrew Tsiyon, the fortified hill of Jerusalem known as the City of David, and by extension Jerusalem, Israel or a promised land. The original meaning of the word is uncertain.

assoc.t: Mount Zion, the biblical hill of Jerusalem
Zion National Park in Utah
Zion, the last human city in The Matrix
Zion Williamson, NBA star

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Tatham: the homestead (ham) of a man named Tata, an Old English personal name of unknown meaning.
namesakes: Tatum O'Neal (youngest Oscar winner, for Paper Moon)

assoc.t: actor Channing Tatum and NBA star Jayson Tatum (surname)

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Louis, from Latin Ludovicus and the Frankish name Hlodowig, built from Germanic words for famous and battle.
As a girls' name, a spelling of Alison, a medieval French pet form of Alice. The double-L form also matches an English surname meaning son of Alan, Alexander or Alice, once used as a boys' name.
namesakes: Allison Janney (actress, The West Wing and Mom)
Allison Williams (actress, Girls and Get Out)

e.etymology: From an English surname that began as a medieval pet form of Elie, the Old French form of Elias or Elijah, Hebrew for my God is Yahweh. As a Scottish surname it may have a separate Gaelic source.
namesakes: Elliott (the boy who befriends E.T. in E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial)

assoc.t: Elliott, the boy who befriends E.T.

e.etymology: A Spanish name of disputed origin. It appears in medieval Latin as Didacus, and is often explained as a shortening of Santiago (Saint James), though the two may be unrelated.

assoc.t: Diego, Dora's cousin in Nick Jr.'s Go, Diego, Go!
Diego, the saber-toothed cat in Ice Age

e.etymology: From the English word melody, ultimately from Greek meloidia, singing. In regular use as a given name since the 20th century.

assoc.t: melody, a musical tune

e.etymology: A phonetic spelling, used since the 1980s, of Schuyler, a surname brought to New York by 17th-century Dutch settlers and usually glossed as scholar. Many parents simply hear sky in it.
namesakes: Skyler White (Walter White's wife on Breaking Bad)

e.meaning: Christmas Day, the birthday of Christ
e.etymology: From Late Latin Natalia, from natalis, of birth, referring to Christmas Day. The name of an early martyr, it is the usual form in Spanish, Italian, Polish and Russian; Natalie is the French form.
namesakes: Natalia Dyer (actress, Nancy in Stranger Things)

e.etymology: A short form of Isabella and Arabella, understood through Italian bella, beautiful. Its US peak followed the Twilight novels, whose heroine is Bella Swan.

assoc.t: Bella Swan, heroine of the Twilight saga

e.note: Also one of the most popular names for female dogs in the US.

e.etymology: A modern simplification of Arianna and Ariane, forms of the Greek name Ariadne, most holy. In myth Ariadne gave Theseus the thread that led him out of the Labyrinth.
namesakes: Ariana DeBose (Oscar-winning actress, West Side Story)

assoc.t: Ariana Grande, pop star

e.etymology: A spelling of Elliott, an English surname that began as a medieval pet form of Elie, the Old French form of Elias or Elijah, Hebrew for my God is Yahweh.
namesakes: Elliot Page (actor, Juno and The Umbrella Academy)
Elliot Stabler (detective on Law and Order: SVU)

e.meaning: wise one; also the sage plant
e.etymology: From the English word sage, both a wise person and the aromatic herb, and from the surname that began as a nickname for a wise man. In general use as a given name since the 1990s.

assoc.t: sage, the cooking herb
a sage, a wise person
sage green, a muted gray-green color

e.etymology: From an English surname, Brice plus -son. Brice is an old name of Celtic origin, known from Saint Brice, a 5th-century bishop of Tours.
A form of Nathanael, altered under the influence of Daniel, from Hebrew Netanel, God has given. In the Gospel of John, Nathanael is one of the first disciples of Jesus.
namesakes: Nathaniel Hawthorne (author of The Scarlet Letter)

e.etymology: From the flower, Old English dægeseage, day's eye. One of the flower names of the 19th century, and also a nickname for Margaret, since French marguerite and Spanish margarita mean daisy.
namesakes: Daisy Buchanan (Gatsby's lost love in The Great Gatsby)
Daisy Ridley (actress, Rey in Star Wars)

assoc.t: daisy, the white-petaled flower
Daisy Duck, Donald Duck's girlfriend
Daisy, sour cream and cottage cheese brand
Princess Daisy of the Super Mario games
Daisy, maker of BB guns

e.etymology: From a Scottish surname that goes back to Grantham in Lincolnshire, Old English grand, gravel, plus ham, homestead.
namesakes: Alexander Graham Bell (inventor of the telephone)

assoc.t: graham crackers, named for Sylvester Graham
